title: Set Matrix Zeroes
pattern: first row/column reused as in-place markers
statement:
You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `matrix`. Whenever a cell holds the value `0`, every cell in the same row and every cell in the same column as that cell must be set to `0` as well.

The rows and columns to clear are decided from the **original** matrix only: a `0` that appears purely because of this clearing must not cause any further row or column to be cleared. Return the resulting matrix.

Because both decisions are taken from the input, the order in which you clear rows and columns does not change the answer.

Constraints: `1 <= matrix.length <= 50`, `1 <= matrix[i].length <= 50` and `-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: One pass to learn which rows and columns matter, a second pass to write, is enough: nothing about the second pass changes the first.
A row that must be cleared can be remembered inside the matrix itself: the first cell of that row is a free flag slot.
The first row and first column are both flag storage and real data, so keep their status in two separate booleans and clear them last.

editorial.approach: The brute force makes one pass to record which rows and which columns hold a zero, using two boolean arrays of length m and n, then writes zeros into a copy of the matrix wherever the row flag or the column flag is set. The optimal version removes those two arrays: it stores the same information inside the matrix itself, writing a marker 0 into matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] for every inner zero at row i, column j. Two booleans keep the status of the first row and the first column, which serve as the marker storage. After the inner cells are cleared from the markers, the first row and column are cleared last from the saved booleans.
editorial.why_optimal: The output itself is m*n cells and every cell must be inspected, so O(m*n) time is unavoidable and both versions achieve it. What differs is memory: the two boolean vectors cost O(m + n), and reusing the first row and column as the marker area drops that to O(1) extra. Since matrix.length and matrix[i].length are both capped at 50, the brute force fits comfortably, but the constant-space variant is the one interviewers ask for.
editorial.pitfalls: Clearing cells in place during the scan is the classic bug: a cell freshly set to 0 then re-zeroes its own row and column, wiping the whole matrix. Reading matrix[0][j] as a marker after phase one without handling the first row separately loses the information for column j when the first row itself should be cleared. The first row and first column need their own booleans, checked before the marker writes overwrite them. Single-row and single-column matrices take no inner-loop iterations at all, so the code must still work when the loops from index 1 never run.
